Small businesses often assume cybersecurity is something only big companies need to worry about. Attackers see it differently. Criminals use automated tools to scan the internet for weak passwords, unpatched software, and exposed systems, and they don't care whether the target is a Fortune 500 firm or a five-person bakery. For a small business, one successful breach can mean stolen customer data, drained bank accounts, or a locked-up point-of-sale system that stops sales for days.

The good news is that most attacks rely on basic gaps that are fixable without a large budget. Turning on multi-factor authentication, using a password manager, keeping software updated, and backing up files to a location that isn't always connected to the network will block the majority of common threats. Training staff to recognize phishing emails, which remain the most frequent way attackers get in, adds another layer of protection that costs little more than an afternoon of attention.

Protecting your business also protects your relationships. Customers, partners, and payment processors increasingly expect reasonable security practices, and a single incident can erode the trust that took years to build. Treating cybersecurity as a routine part of running the business, rather than an emergency to deal with later, lets you keep serving your customers with confidence.
